newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Mahathir's party disqualifies seven poll hopefuls.
newsitem.headline: Mahathir's party disqualifies seven poll hopefuls.

text.p: Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on Monday disqualified seven candidates from contesting party elections in his United Malays National Organisation (UMNO).

Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the candidates were disqualified for trying to buy votes and for violating UMNO's blanket ban on campaigning for Thursday's polls at the party's triennial election assembly.
"We had to make it clear that we not only give warnings...we also act," Anwar, Mahathir's deputy in both the government and UMNO, told reporters after announcing the disqualifications.
UMNO is the main party in the ruling National Front coalition, which has governed Malaysia since its independence from Britain in 1957.

Political analysts say the UMNO polls are arguably more significant than general elections, which the National Front has always won in a landslide. By political convention, the president and deputy president of UMNO become Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister.
Mahathir and Anwar are unchallenged for the top two jobs in UMNO under a pact made at last year's convention.
But 185 candidates are contesting other positions, including three vice presidencies, 30 seats on the policy-making Supreme Council, and heads of the youth and women's wings of the party.
Six of those disqualified were contesting Supreme Council seats, Anwar said.

He identified them as Mohamed Shariff Omar -- deputy chief minister of the northern Penang state and the most senior of the six -- and Salamon Salamat, Mohamed Aini Taib, Latif Mirasa, Abdul Malek Hanapiah and Adam Abdul Hamid.
The seventh man, Ayub Mat Aris, was contesting an executive council position in the youth wing, Anwar said.
Mahathir announced the ban on campaigning in an effort to curb what he said was a growing trend toward vote-buying and other malpractices commonly referred to as "money politics."
But the prime minister on Sunday lamented that despite his warnings, money politics appeared to have become an "institution" in UMNO.

"That is why we should take whatever action to ensure criminals do not become leaders. If we fail in this effort, our future will be bleak," he said in a written message in the convention's souvenir programme.
